actions.justification: MANDATORY: Immediate stroke team activation is required for this acute ischemic stroke presentation. Time-critical coordination for CT imaging, tPA eligibility assessment, and potential thrombectomy requires the full stroke team. This is the first mandatory action per protocol.
MANDATORY: IV access is essential for medication administration including potential tPA, fluids, and other acute interventions. Must be established immediately at time of arrival.

Critical first assessment step per AHA stroke guidelines. BP is 165/95 — below the 185/110 tPA threshold but requires monitoring. Neurological status assessment is needed to establish baseline NIHSS and guide treatment decisions.
MANDATORY action per current phase. ECG is essential in acute stroke workup to identify atrial fibrillation (cardioembolic source) or other arrhythmias. Must be completed within 60-minute deadline.

Immediate interpretation of the 12-lead ECG is needed to identify atrial fibrillation or other cardiac arrhythmias that could be the embolic source of this posterior circulation stroke, and to guide anticoagulation decisions.

SpO2 is 97% — while not critically hypoxic, supplemental oxygen monitoring is appropriate in acute stroke. Per AHA guidelines, oxygen should be administered if SpO2 falls below 94%. Ordering now ensures readiness if saturation drops.

Troponin is indicated in acute ischemic stroke to evaluate for cardioembolic source (atrial fibrillation, ACS) and assess for concomitant cardiac injury. Elevated troponin is seen in posterior circulation strokes and guides further cardiac workup.

Obtaining cardiac history helps assess for cardioembolic etiology of stroke (e.g., ACS with cardioembolic stroke, aortic dissection as stroke mimic) and identifies contraindications to thrombolysis such as recent MI or aortic dissection.

Patient with acute posterior circulation ischemic stroke and elevated BP (165/95 mmHg) with history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Cardiology consult warranted to evaluate for cardioembolic source (atrial fibrillation, structural heart disease) and to assist with BP management prior to potential tPA administration (target <185/110 mmHg).

Aspirin loading (325 mg) is indicated for acute ischemic stroke per AHA guidelines as antiplatelet therapy. Should be administered after hemorrhagic stroke has been excluded on CT. This is a time-critical intervention for acute ischemic stroke management.

Patient has posterior circulation stroke symptoms (vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia). Comparing with prior ECG may help identify atrial fibrillation or other cardioembolic sources relevant to stroke etiology and anticoagulation decisions.

With suspected posterior circulation ischemic stroke and elevated BP (165/95), anticoagulation consideration is relevant for cardioembolic etiology. However, this must be weighed carefully - CT head needed first to rule out hemorrhage. Flagging for review pending imaging results.

Right-sided ECG can help identify right ventricular involvement and provide additional cardiac workup in the context of stroke with hypertension and hyperlipidemia, supporting comprehensive cardioembolic workup.

NIHSS score is essential for quantifying stroke severity, guiding tPA eligibility, and documenting neurological baseline for this posterior circulation stroke presentation (vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, gait ataxia). Required per AHA stroke guidelines before thrombolysis decision.

Determining the exact time of last known well is critical for tPA eligibility assessment. The 4.5-hour treatment window requires precise onset time calculation. Patient is at 70 minutes since arrival but onset time needs confirmation.
Maintain IV access and hemodynamic support while completing stroke workup. Avoid large fluid boluses but ensure adequate perfusion pressure for ischemic penumbra.

Non-contrast CT head is the critical next step to rule out hemorrhage before any thrombolysis decision. Patient is at 80 minutes - still within tPA window but CT must be obtained urgently. BP is 165/95 which is below the 185/110 threshold for tPA contraindication.

CTA of head and neck is indicated to evaluate for large vessel occlusion (posterior circulation given diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia - basilar artery occlusion must be ruled out) and determine if mechanical thrombectomy is needed.
Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke symptoms and must be ruled out before any thrombolytic therapy. This is a critical early step per AHA stroke guidelines (target within 10 minutes of arrival).

Patient presents with posterior circulation stroke symptoms (vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia). MRI DWI is superior for detecting posterior fossa/brainstem ischemia that may be CT-negative, and will help confirm diagnosis and guide tPA/thrombectomy eligibility.
PT/INR and PTT are required before tPA eligibility can be confirmed. Coagulation status must be assessed to rule out anticoagulation contraindications per AHA stroke guidelines.
Platelet count is a mandatory component of tPA eligibility checklist. Thrombocytopenia (<100,000) is a contraindication to IV alteplase.

Neurology consult is critical for this posterior circulation stroke presentation (vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia). At 110 minutes from arrival, tPA eligibility decision must be made urgently within the 4.5-hour window. Neurology should confirm diagnosis, review CT/CTA/MRI results, assess for contraindications, and guide thrombolysis or thrombectomy decisions.

Patient is at 110 minutes from arrival with acute ischemic stroke symptoms. If CT head rules out hemorrhage, BP is controlled to <185/110, and no contraindications exist (coagulation labs ordered, CBC ordered), IV alteplase 0.9mg/kg should be administered per AHA guidelines within the 4.5-hour window. Note: BP is currently 165/95 which is within acceptable range for tPA. Anticoagulation was already given - this must be reviewed as a potential contraindication before administration.
